title: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
desc: Integrates legal analysis, practical judgment, verification, interdisciplinary work and deliberate practice while asking who funds apprenticeship.

kps.k: AI renews a longstanding argument for integrating legal analysis, practical competence and professional responsibility—not simply adding technology courses.
kps.d: The cluster centres on how schools and employers should develop lawyers for changing practice. Wilkins, Tellmann and the Carnegie summary argue that analytical instruction remains valuable but does not adequately prepare students to solve clients’ problems, exercise ethical judgment or work in institutions. Perlin predicts that legal reasoning will become more important with AI. Furlong calls for a more fundamental overhaul of education and licensing, while still preserving analytical foundations. The disagreement concerns the scale and purpose of reform more than whether foundational legal knowledge matters.

qs.q: Law schools fail to complement the focus on skill in legal analyses with effective support for developing  ethical and social skills.
qs.a: Educating Lawyers: Preparation for the Profession of Law (Summary) · Academia · 2007

kps.k: Pressure on apprenticeship raises a contested question: who should provide and pay for professional development?
kps.d: Westfahl and Wilkins argue that the traditional division—schools teach legal thinking, firms teach practice—no longer fits clients’ multidisciplinary demands and resistance to funding junior training. Tellmann similarly claims that firms increasingly cannot or will not maintain their training role; the Vanderbilt discussion asks how students will learn if foundational junior tasks disappear. Hoffman counters that demands for practice-ready graduates can offload employers’ responsibilities onto schools and lack a stable target. These accounts identify a training risk, not a measured collapse of apprenticeship or an established replacement model.

qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

qs.q: The thing that’s interesting to me is whether it’s taking place outside of law school that directly impacts it is that we are messing with that guild model of knowledge work and we are taking away a lot of those ⁓ foundational sort of bricklaying skills that used to be done by first and second year associates that’s increasingly getting commoditized and being shrunk down to zero.
qs.a: Tiara Time and Data Center Politics: Vanderbilt’s AI Governance Playbook with Cat Moon and Mark Williams · Academia · 2026

kps.k: AI readiness spans transferable learning skills, hands-on use and the judgment to reject or verify a system.
kps.d: Perlin and O’Leary prioritise tool-agnostic methods for approaching unfamiliar technology and improving workflows. Smith and Logvinova put more emphasis on understanding AI and practising with available platforms. Wakeling offers a concrete teaching approach: students should justify whether AI fits the task, explain their prompts, and check and correct its output; declining unsuitable AI can merit high marks. These positions differ in emphasis rather than necessarily conflict. Hoffman questions whether rapidly changing employer demands can define a workable curriculum, while McCormack stresses that students need legal sources and substantive foundations to use tools professionally.

qs.q: I think it’s a good goal for them to be able to have those next-level conversations, but instead I think we need to give them the meta-skills of: How do I deal with a brand-new tool?
qs.a: How AI Is Changing Legal Education with Dyane O'Leary and Jonah Perlin — full episode transcript · Academia · 2025

qs.q: And I think law schools should make sure that they’re incorporating AI into their way of working, right — the way that they would offer different tools like Lexis and Westlaw.
qs.a: Inside Legal Innovation: AI Adoption with Jae Um & Ilona Logvinova — full episode transcript · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Interdisciplinary problem-solving and human relationships supply the main positive account of future lawyer competence.
kps.d: Wilkins argues that problems such as cybersecurity, sustainability and geopolitical risk require lawyers to help define problems and develop solutions with other professionals, not merely answer isolated legal questions. Proposed competencies include business and data fluency, systems thinking, empathy, teamwork, leadership and cross-cultural understanding. Furlong emphasises trustworthy judgment under uncertainty and early client-facing experience. Hoffman qualifies claims that judgment is uniquely human: he expects LLMs to perform some predictive tasks, while seeing counselling and navigation of complexity as increasingly important. These are accounts of likely professional value, not proof that particular tasks or jobs will remain protected.

qs.q: All these changes are pushing law from a “fee for service” model,” in which clients bring lawyers “legal questions,” and lawyers provide “legal answers” which the client then implements, to what I’ve been calling an “integrated solutions model.” In this model, neither the contours of the problem nor the possible array of solutions is strictly “legal” or fully understood by either the client or the lawyer.
qs.a: The legal profession in 2024: The wider view · Academia · 2024

qs.q: The purpose of a lawyer is to deliver reliable, trustworthy judgment and under conditions of uncertainty.
qs.a: The Future of Law Firm Business Models in the Age of AI — Jordan Furlong on the Lawyerist Podcast (ep. 607) · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The proposed alternative is coordinated, lifelong development with deliberate practice and feedback.
kps.d: Westfahl and Wilkins propose shared responsibility among schools, firms and corporate clients for legal expertise, transferable professional skills and career-building relationships, with clients financing only part of the effort. Moon adds students to the design process and rejects unilateral demands from either practitioners or educators. Practical proposals include integrated skills-and-doctrine teaching, stronger clinics and practitioner teaching, team-based assessment, experimentation and continuing education partnerships. Westfahl and Wilkins suggest making at least one-third of courses, assignments and assessments team-based. These remain proposed designs rather than a validated common model.

qs.q: 151 To be effective, this collaboration must concentrate on helping lawyers build three critical capacities: technical legal skills and expertise, professional skills that are adaptable to any professional context, and opportunity-generating networks of relationships.
qs.a: The Leadership Imperative: A Collaborative Approach to Professional Development in the Global Age of More for Less · Academia · 2017

qs.q: And as legal education is figuring out what are we best prepared and suited to provide and what do we need to change, there’s so much room in the middle, right, for the stakeholders and I would also say students.
qs.a: Tiara Time and Data Center Politics: Vanderbilt’s AI Governance Playbook with Cat Moon and Mark Williams · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Evidence shows curricular activity, but does not establish which reforms improve competence or career outcomes.
kps.d: Smith reports an ABA survey completed by 29 deans or faculty members between December 2023 and mid-February 2024: among responding schools, 55% offered AI classes, 83% offered curricular opportunities to learn AI use and 69% had changed academic-integrity policies. These figures describe respondents, not all schools, and measure provision rather than effectiveness. Westfahl and Wilkins cite positive correlations between clinical education and preparedness, not causal proof of their full model. Classroom observations, institutional examples and proposed customised-GPT feedback illustrate possibilities; claimed learning, inclusion and wellbeing benefits remain prospective. Leonard accordingly calls for testing approaches and sharing successes and failures.

qs.q: This survey was completed by 29 law school deans or faculty members between December 2023 and mid-February 2024.
qs.a: A Problem-Solving Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: I think we need to start really understanding and trying and testing and taking new approaches – and like you said, sharing across silos what we’re learning and what we need more of and what’s working and what’s not.
qs.a: ChatGPT Gets an A+: What That Means for Law School, Workflows, and Your Everyday Life — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Institutional incentives may obstruct reform even when new skills attract broad support.
kps.d: Wilkins notes that faculty autonomy enables new courses but tenure and academic freedom complicate removing existing content. McCormack identifies regulatory, administrative, alumni and student constraints. Um urges employers and applicants to scrutinise curricula rather than rely on prestige; Tellmann allows different balances of conceptual and vocational preparation according to institutional mission. Leonard questions whether recruiting more entrepreneurial and collaborative students can succeed if workplace incentives remain unchanged. Faster change is possible in Barnwell’s account of enterprise resource pressure, but Wilkins’s longitudinal career-research example and Taking the Long View caution that disruption can coexist with enduring hierarchies.

qs.q: Because you are taking away a professor’s ability to teach what they want, which – in a world in which professors have academic freedom and tenure – is extremely difficult to do.
qs.a: An Interview with Professor David B. Wilkins · Academia · 2023

qs.q: I think that it is time to start asking about the curriculum at some of these law schools in a systematic way.
qs.a: Inside Legal Innovation: AI Adoption with Jae Um & Ilona Logvinova — full episode transcript · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Professional preparation serves public purposes as well as employer demand.
kps.d: Wilkins grounds professional legitimacy in independence and commitment to the public good, while asking whether schools should accommodate, resist or shape markets. Smith advocates civics, ethical judgment and service to people lacking legal help. The Carnegie summary and Reimagining Langdell’s Legacy seek integration of moral reflection, practical work and inclusive education rather than training solely for immediate billability. Wilkins links more affordable skill development to access to justice and argues for institutional redesign to support inclusion. Debt, wellbeing and trust therefore belong to the reform agenda, not merely its recruitment strategy. These normative commitments do not establish that AI or curricular reform will close the civil justice gap.

qs.q: One of the answers, he concluded, is that “clients need the legitimacy of lawyers who are themselves legitimate.” The idea that lawyers are independent and have some commitment to the public good means they bring something to the table “you can’t get from your public relations specialist.”  *– Greg DiBella*
qs.a: In chair lecture, Wilkins discusses educating global lawyers · Academia · 2010

qs.q: Another important area that law schools should focus on is teaching civics.
qs.a: A Problem-Solving Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: This legal-tech-vendor source does not reject the need to develop different capabilities, but it shifts the principal explanation and priority away from coordinated, lifelong competence reform. Barnwell argues that enterprise resource constraints, demands for data-informed value, and machine-enabled delivery may force change faster than reform proceeding through law school, the associate tournament, and eventual institutional leadership. A second strand stresses that attracting entrepreneurial and collaborative entrants will not succeed if professional incentives, culture, and workplace structures remain unchanged. The internal variation is therefore between an external economic-and-technological mechanism for rapid change and an internal cultural barrier to integrating differently skilled lawyers. Both redirect attention from curriculum and shared apprenticeship funding toward the operating model and incentives of legal work. These are experience-based expectations and questions, not quantified evidence that enterprise pressure will produce better lawyer competence or replace coordinated development.

qs.q: Those are the macro patterns I’m seeing that make me think the rate of change may not be predicated on somebody learning this in school, surviving the tournament, and eventually getting enough power to institutionalize it decades from now.
qs.a: Jason Barnwell — Agiloft (CLO, ex-Microsoft) on AI agents, declared protocols, and the rate of change in legal · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: But how frustrated would one of those people be if they were selected and then plugged into a model that hasn’t changed at all?
qs.a: Jason Barnwell — Agiloft (CLO, ex-Microsoft) on AI agents, declared protocols, and the rate of change in legal · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an:
Across this curated set, the academia and research voice accepts the synthesis’s principal proposition that AI renews—not originates—the need to integrate analytical foundations with practical judgment, professional responsibility and interdisciplinary competence. It materially develops that proposition through concrete proposals: transparent curriculum review; integrated doctrine-and-skills teaching; clinics, practitioner instruction and team-based assessment; tool-agnostic technological adaptability; broader competencies in business, data, design, empathy and collaboration; and shared, career-long responsibility among law schools, firms, corporate clients and students. Several sources also extend the rationale beyond employer demand to inclusion, institutional practice, access to justice, democratic responsibility and professional legitimacy.

Material variation concerns emphasis, institutional responsibility and confidence rather than the reform’s basic direction. Some sources foreground AI and changing junior work, while older work identifies the same educational imbalance independently of generative AI. Westfahl and Wilkins offer the most developed lifelong model, including partial client funding; Moon adds students to collaborative redesign. Tellmann places greater responsibility on law schools as firm apprenticeship weakens, whereas Hoffman warns that demands for “AI-ready” graduates may offload employers’ training obligations and provide an unstable curricular target. Perlin, O’Leary and McCormack prioritise enduring legal foundations and transferable methods over instruction tied to current tools. Wilkins’s work broadens competence toward multidisciplinary and institutional problem-solving, while the legal-conservatism sources caution that disruption may be absorbed by existing hierarchies; one of those sources redirects attention toward preserving public values and studying institutional inertia rather than endorsing a specific training programme.

The evidence base remains a significant qualification. These sources primarily provide normative arguments, conceptual frameworks, institutional observations and forecasts. They identify risks to apprenticeship and propose reforms, but generally do not establish through measured outcomes which interventions improve competence or careers. AI-specific verification receives limited direct treatment, and the question of who ultimately funds replacement apprenticeship remains unresolved despite the partial-funding proposal. These limitations do not reverse the overall position; they make the contribution an elaboration of the proposition rather than empirical confirmation of a settled model.

qs.q: 151 To be effective, this collaboration must concentrate on helping lawyers build three critical capacities: technical legal skills and expertise, professional skills that are adaptable to any professional context, and opportunity-generating networks of relationships.
qs.a: The Leadership Imperative: A Collaborative Approach to Professional Development in the Global Age of More for Less · Academia · 2017

qs.q: Similarly, all faculty should take a holistic view of the competencies required for ethical lawyering and commit to incorporating a wide range of skills along with the doctrinal content already covered in their classes.
qs.a: Reimagining Langdell's Legacy: Puncturing the Equilibrium in Law School Pedagogy · Academia · 2023

vlens.an: These curated market-analyst, consultancy and press sources accept the proposition that AI renews the case for integrating legal analysis with practical judgment and responsible technology use, and they materially extend it in several ways. Common reasons include concern that the traditional school–firm division of training is becoming less viable, pressure from changing legal-service business models and employer expectations, and the need to prepare lawyers to use AI discerningly rather than merely adding generic technology instruction. Wakeling supplies the most concrete AI pedagogy: assess whether a system is fit for the task, justify prompting choices, and verify and correct outputs. Furlong gives reform an organising professional purpose—trustworthy judgment under uncertainty—while coupling analytical foundations with early experience listening to and understanding people. Logvinova, Um and Leonard add ecosystem and institutional perspectives, including hands-on platform access, scrutiny of curricula, and the practice–academia divide. Material variation concerns the scale and emphasis of reform: Furlong advocates fundamental restructuring of education and licensing; Wakeling focuses narrowly on classroom judgment, prompting and verification; and the Inside Legal Innovation discussion stresses commercial pressures, employer power and institutional incentives. These sources do not develop the synthesis’s coordinated lifelong-development model or resolve who should fund apprenticeship. Their claims are also chiefly recommendations, observations and forecasts, not evidence that particular reforms improve competence or career outcomes; their inclusion should not be read as representing all analysts, consultancies or press voices.

qs.q: And the third thing is that you’re still applying critical thinking and you are validating and taking the best and fixing the worst of the AI output.
qs.a: Talking about the Future of AI in Law with David Wakeling · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The selected regulators, courts and professional-body voices accept the synthesis’s core proposition that AI-era lawyer development must combine legal foundations with practical judgment, ethics, human capabilities and continuing learning. They materially extend it by framing competence reform as a coordinated institutional and public-purpose project: law schools, employers and continuing-education bodies should collaborate; curricula should incorporate practical AI use, experiential learning and formative feedback; and reform should advance civics, inclusion and access to justice as well as employability. Internal variation is mainly one of emphasis. Some sources focus on lifelong learning, interpersonal skills and technology as augmentation; others propose concrete mechanisms such as customised GPT feedback, applicant curriculum checklists and cross-institutional experimentation. Wilkins reaches further toward institutional redesign, paraprofessional delivery and systemic reform, while other contributions remain centred on law-school curricula. The sources also vary evidentially: reported curricular provision and qualitative observations show activity, but many claimed benefits are predictions or proposals rather than demonstrated improvements in competence or careers. Collectively, they give less attention to verification practices and do not resolve who should fund apprenticeship. This assessment concerns only the curated sources supplied and does not imply that they represent all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: They must not only instill traditional lawyering skills such as problem-solving and judgment, but they also need to acknowledge and support the reality that lawyers of the future will need to incorporate AI tools into legal service delivery.
qs.a: A Problem-Solving Profession · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: The only way we can preserve the core principles of the legal profession and excellence in practice, while at the same time advancing to become more diverse and provide more service to broader constituencies is by coming together to effectuate systemic change.
qs.a: Legal Trios: Reflecting on the Legal Profession with Prof. David Wilkins at Annual Meeting · Regulators & courts · 2016

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources support the principal proposition by establishing that reform of lawyer development predates generative AI. Their common argument is that legal analysis remains necessary but is insufficient when separated from practical judgment, client-centred problem-solving, ethical formation, institutional competence and public responsibility. They therefore supply the foundations for the synthesis’s claim that AI renews, rather than originates, the case for integrated professional preparation. Material variation lies in emphasis: the Carnegie summary focuses on the imbalance between analytical instruction, apprenticeship-like practice and professional responsibility; Wilkins stresses institutional practice, professional independence and public legitimacy while remaining uncertain about which organisational models will prevail; and the legal-technology source goes further by adding technology, user-oriented design and entrepreneurship, although its claimed opportunities are prospective. Collectively, these sources do not address generative-AI verification, the possible disappearance of junior tasks, or a coordinated model for funding lifelong development, so they support the synthesis’s educational and public-purpose core without establishing its AI-specific or apprenticeship-financing components.

qs.q: Most law schools give only casual attention to teaching students how to use legal thinking in the  complexity of actual law practice.
qs.a: Educating Lawyers: Preparation for the Profession of Law (Summary) · Academia · 2007

qs.q: Design and aesthetic is the  key to developing the sort of solutions that help solve the real problems of end users.
qs.a: Quantitative Legal Prediction — or — How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Start Preparing for the Data-Driven Future of the Legal Services Industry · Academia · 2013

elens.an:
The 2015–2022 sources accept the proposition’s core and provide much of its pre-generative-AI foundation. Across this curated set, they preserve legal analysis while arguing that lawyer development must also encompass practical problem-solving, ethical judgment, technology fluency, interdisciplinary collaboration and durable human relationships. Their material extension is institutional: development should be lifelong and jointly supported by law schools, firms and corporate clients rather than left to the traditional school-versus-apprenticeship division. They also broaden the rationale beyond employer readiness to include inclusion, access to justice and adaptation across an integrated legal-services ecosystem.

There is meaningful variation in emphasis. Westfahl and Wilkins offer the most concrete shared-development model, including partial client funding, team-based experiential learning and transferable professional capacities. The Wilkins account puts greater weight on institutional redesign, professional integrity, inclusion and access to justice, while remaining cautious about whether observed pressures constitute a lasting paradigm shift. The integrated-services source focuses more on collaboration among lawyers, other professionals and technology, predicts that AI will replace some jobs while human expertise remains important, and adds evidence-based regulation of traditional, alternative and hybrid delivery models.

These sources do not fully anticipate the later proposition’s specific emphasis on generative-AI verification. Nor do they establish through outcome evidence that their proposed curricula or institutional models improve competence. Their principal contributions are arguments, designs and qualified predictions: they materially develop the broader reform agenda that AI later renews, rather than validating a settled model.

qs.q: But these humans must be taught to work effectively with new technologies, in environments where lawyers and other professionals and knowledge workers (whom we should stop calling “nonlawyers”) must learn to collaborate effectively to deliver value to increasingly sophisticated and cost-conscious clients.
qs.a: Taking the “Alternative” Out of Alternative Legal Service Providers · Academia · 2019

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core claim that generative AI renews, rather than creates, the need to integrate doctrinal analysis with practical judgment, ethical responsibility, interdisciplinary collaboration and continuing development. They materially extend it by proposing transparent curriculum review, inclusive and integrated teaching, practical AI instruction, customised-GPT formative feedback, applicant-facing curriculum checklists and stronger employer pressure for reform. Common reasons include the limits of doctrine-only and individually oriented instruction, the growth of multidisciplinary client problems, rapidly changing technology, and the continued importance of human judgment, relationships and public responsibility. Material variation concerns emphasis and confidence: some sources offer concrete educational designs, whereas others only call for preparation; some expect AI to augment lawyers, while Wilkins leaves staffing effects open; and the evidence of curricular activity among 29 responding schools does not demonstrate improved competence or career outcomes. The institutional accounts also differ: one treats professional conservatism principally as a barrier supporting the proposition, while another redirects attention toward conservatism’s legitimate role in preserving democracy, the rule of law and liberty. Taken as a curated set rather than a representative survey, the period therefore builds on the proposition without establishing a validated reform model, a collapse of apprenticeship or settled employment effects.

qs.q: Similarly, all faculty should take a holistic view of the competencies required for ethical lawyering and commit to incorporating a wide range of skills along with the doctrinal content already covered in their classes.
qs.a: Reimagining Langdell's Legacy: Puncturing the Equilibrium in Law School Pedagogy · Academia · 2023

qs.q: The world is changing too quickly to have three static years of your life prepare you for the rest of your profession.
qs.a: AI's Impact on Legal Education: Preparing Future Lawyers for a Tech-Driven World — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources broadly accept the proposition that AI renews the need to integrate foundational legal reasoning with practical judgment, adaptable learning, interdisciplinary collaboration and responsible AI use. They materially develop it by supplying more concrete accounts of implementation: hands-on access to AI platforms; tool-agnostic preparation for unfamiliar systems; teaching students to decide when AI is unsuitable and to verify and correct its output; multidisciplinary, human-AI decision-making frameworks; and experimentation shared among law schools, firms and other stakeholders. Common reasons include accelerating automation, changing client and business-model expectations, complex problems that cannot be resolved through legal analysis alone, and the continuing importance of empathy, teamwork and critical judgment under an augmentation rather than replacement model. Internal variation concerns emphasis and evidentiary confidence. Perlin, O’Leary and McCormack prioritise durable legal foundations and transferable meta-skills; Logvinova stresses earlier practical access to current tools; Wakeling offers the most specific verification-centred pedagogy; Wilkins broadens competence toward integrated solutions and institutional resilience; Leonard emphasises cross-institutional testing rather than a settled model. Some contributors predict widespread adoption or intensified employer pressure, whereas others explicitly acknowledge uncertainty and institutional constraints. These sources provide observations, recommendations and early experiments, not evidence that adoption is universal or that the proposed reforms improve competence or career outcomes. They also do not resolve the proposition’s contested apprenticeship-funding question.

qs.q: And the third thing is that you’re still applying critical thinking and you are validating and taking the best and fixing the worst of the AI output.
qs.a: Talking about the Future of AI in Law with David Wakeling · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: I think we need to start really understanding and trying and testing and taking new approaches – and like you said, sharing across silos what we’re learning and what we need more of and what’s working and what’s not.
qs.a: ChatGPT Gets an A+: What That Means for Law School, Workflows, and Your Everyday Life — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively support the proposition that AI renews—rather than creates—the need to reform lawyer development across legal analysis, practical judgment, human relationships and continuing professional learning. Common reasons include erosion of junior apprenticeship work, a persistent gap between law schools and employers, rapidly changing and ill-defined demands for “AI-ready” graduates, and the growing value attributed to counseling, adaptability and judgment under uncertainty. Material variation concerns emphasis and scale: Tellmann preserves rigorous analytical foundations while adding practical, technological and interdisciplinary competence; Furlong advocates more fundamental education and licensing reform organised around trustworthy judgment; Moon adds collaborative design involving educators, practitioners and students; Leonard stresses flexible partnerships with continuing-education providers; and the justice-focused source foregrounds experiential learning and public purpose while saying little about AI-specific competence. Hoffman supports reassessing education but cautions that schools cannot chase an unstable technological target and that employers may be offloading training responsibilities. Barnwell redirects attention toward enterprise resource constraints, machine-enabled delivery and professional incentives as potentially faster forces for change than curricular reform. These differences qualify the route and institutional allocation of responsibility, but they do not amount to an overall rejection. Across the sources, claims about future competence and institutional change are mostly recommendations, observations or provisional forecasts rather than measured evidence that particular reforms improve outcomes.

qs.q: The way forward  As law schools assume greater responsibility for preparing lawyers for the GC 4.0  environment, they must clarify their purpose and commit to developing graduates  with both analytical depth and practical skills competence.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

qs.q: There is such a gap, especially in the handoff between schools and employers, and especially because of the confusion that AI has created across those groups, that we really need new models — and models that are capable of being flexible.
